<!-- lem-1: body_md -->
\label{lem 2.1}
The $p$-curvature functions define automorphisms of the discrete flat connection $(L_m)$.
That is, for $1 \leqslant l, m \leqslant n$, we have:
\begin{equation}
\label{c2}
C_l(k + f_m) L_m(k) = L_m(k) C_l(k).
\end{equation}
Furthermore, the $p$-curvature functions mutually commute:
\begin{equation}
\label{c3}
C_l(k) C_m(k) = C_m(k) C_l(k),
\end{equation}
and the $p$-curvature functions are $p$-periodic:
\begin{equation}
\label{c4}
C_l(k+pf_m) = C_l(k), \qquad 1\leqslant l,m\leqslant n.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lem-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Formula
$\eqref{c2}$ follows by repeatedly applying
$$L_l(k+f_m)L_m(k)=L_m(k+f_l)L_l(k)$$
to move $L_m(k)$ through the $p$-step product. One obtains
$$C_l(k+f_m)L_m(k)
=
L_m(k)C_l(k).$$
For commutativity, compare parallel transport along the two $p\times p$ rectangles:
$$
C_l(k+pf_m)C_m(k)
=
C_m(k+pf_l)C_l(k).
$$
Using $p$-periodicity gives
$$C_l(k)C_m(k)=C_m(k)C_l(k).$$
Finally, $\eqref{c4}$ follows immediately from the $p$-periodicity of $L_l$\,.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lem-2: body_md -->
\label{lem 2.2}
The $p$-curvature functions $(\tilde \varphi_l, \tilde\psi_m)$ are constant,
that is, independent of $(j,k)$.
<!-- end lem-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Since the connection has rank one, the operators are scalar. Applying
\eqref{c2} in each of the $e_i$- and $f_m$-directions gives
\[
\widetilde\varphi_l(j+e_i,k)=\widetilde\varphi_l(j,k),\qquad
\widetilde\varphi_l(j,k+f_m)=\widetilde\varphi_l(j,k),
\]
and similarly
\[
\widetilde\psi_m(j+e_i,k)=\widetilde\psi_m(j,k),\qquad
\widetilde\psi_m(j,k+f_i)=\widetilde\psi_m(j,k).
\]
Hence all these functions are constant.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lem-3: body_md -->
\label{lem int d}

 that the rank-one discrete connection satisfies
\[
\widetilde\varphi_l=1,\qquad l=1,\dots,r.
\]
 Let
$u:{\mathbb Z}^{r+n} \to V_{\mathbb K}$ be a $p$-periodic function.
Then
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{ili d}
\int \left(\varphi_l(j,k)\,u(j+e_l,k) - u(j,k)\right) dj = 0
\end{eqnarray}
for all $k\in{\mathbb Z}^n$ and $l=1,\dots,r$.
<!-- end lem-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
We prove \eqref{ili d} for $l=1$. The proof for other $l$ is similar.
The key identity is:$$\mu_{(0,0),(j,k)}\,\varphi_l(j,k)
=
\mu_{(0,0),(j+e_l,k)}.$$
This follows from the transport convention introduced earlier: $\varphi_l(j,k)$ transports from $(j+e_l,k)$ to $(j,k)$. Since the connection is rank one, the factors commute, so the order is immaterial.  

For $l=1$, we  have
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{d1}
&&
\int \varphi_1(j,k)\,u(j+e_1,k) d j
=
\sum_{i_1, \dots, i_r=0}^{p-1}
\varphi_1(i_1e_1+ \dots+ i_re_r,k)
\\
\notag
&&
\times \ \
u((i_1+1)e_1 + i_2e_2+ \dots +i_re_r, k)
\ \mu_{(0,0),( i_1e_1+\dots + i_re_r,k)}\,
\\
\notag
&&
=
\sum_{i_1, \dots, i_r=0}^{p-1}
u((i_1+1)e_1+i_2e_2+ \dots + i_re_r, k) \,\mu_{(0,0),((i_1+1)e_1+i_2e_2+\dots+i_re_r,k)}\,.
\end{eqnarray}
This sum equals
\begin{eqnarray*}
&&
\int u(j,k) dj
=
\sum_{i_1, \dots, i_r=0}^{p-1}
u(i_1e_1+i_2e_2+ \dots +i_re_r,k)
\mu_{(0,0),(i_1e_1+i_2e_2+\dots+i_re_r,k)}\,,
\end{eqnarray*}
since for any $i_2, \dots, i_r$ we have
\begin{eqnarray*}
&&
u(pe_1+i_2e_2+ \dots+i_re_r,k)
=
u(i_2e_2+\dots+i_re_r, k),
\end{eqnarray*}
because $u$ is $p$-periodic,
and
\begin{eqnarray*}
\mu_{(0,0),(pe_1+i_2e_2+\dots+i_re_r,k)}
&=&
\mu_{(0,0),(i_2e_2+\dots + i_re_r,k)}\, \tilde \varphi_1(i_2e_2+\dots +i_re_r, k)
\\
&= &
\mu_{(0,0),(i_2e_2+\dots+i_re_r,k)} ,
\end{eqnarray*}
due
to the assumption that $\tilde \varphi_1=1$.
The lemma is proved.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
\label{thm sol}

If the $p$-invariant discrete flat connection
$(\varphi_l,\psi_m)$ is special, then $I$ is a flat section
 of the $p$-invariant discrete flat connection $(L_m)$,
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{ili}
I(k+f_m) = L_m(k) I(k),
\end{eqnarray}
for all $k\in{\mathbb Z}^n$ and $m=1,\dots, n$.
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
We prove relation \eqref{ili} for $m=1$. The proof for other $m$ is similar.
We have
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{IR1}
\phantom{aaa}
\psi_1(j,k) \,w(j,k+f_1) \,= \,L_1(k)\,w(j,k) +
\sum_{l=1}^r \left(\varphi_l(j,k)\,g_{l,1}(j+e_l,k) - g_{l,1}(j,k)\right)
\end{eqnarray}
by assumption. We send each term $T(j,k)$ of this identity
to the element $\int T(j,k) dj\in V_{\mathbb K}$.
In particular, the left-hand side is sent to
\begin{eqnarray*}
&&
\int \psi_1(j,k) \,w(j, k+f_1) dj
=
\sum_{i_1, \dots, i_r=0}^{p-1}
w(i_1e_1+ \dots +i_re_r, k+f_1)
\\
&&
\times\ \
\psi_1(i_1e_1+\dots+ i_re_r,k)\,
\mu_{(0,0),(i_1e_1+\dots+ i_re_r,k)}
\\
&&
=
\sum_{i_1, \dots, i_r=0}^{p-1}
w(i_1e_1+\dots+ i_re_r,k+f_1)\,
\mu_{(0,0),(i_1e_1+\dots+ i_re_r,k+f_1)}
=
I(k+f_1).
\end{eqnarray*}
The first term on the right-hand side is sent to
\begin{eqnarray*}
\int L_1(k)w(j,k) dj =
L_1(k)\int w(j,k) dj
=
L_1(k)\,I(k).
\end{eqnarray*}
Each summand in the final sum in in \eqref{IR1} vanishes by
 Lemma \ref{lem int d}. Relation
\eqref{ili} is proved for $m=1$. Theorem \ref{thm sol} is proved.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- thm-2: body_md -->
\label{thm i sol}

The flat section $I : {\mathbb Z}^n \to V_{\mathbb K}$ of Theorem \ref{thm sol}, if nonzero,  is an eigensection of the $p$-curvature functions:
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{e so}
C_m(k)I(k) = \tilde \psi_m(0,0)I(k),
\end{eqnarray}
for $k\in{\mathbb Z}^n$ and $m=1,\dots,n$.
<!-- end thm-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
We have $C_m(k)I(k)= I(k +pf_m)$ and
\begin{eqnarray*}
I(k +pf_m)
&=&
\sum_{i_1, \dots, i_r=0}^{p-1}
w(i_1e_1+\dots + i_re_r, k+pf_m)\, \mu_{(0,0),(i_1e_1+\dots +i_re_r,k+pf_m)}.
\end{eqnarray*}
We have
\begin{eqnarray*}
w(i_1e_1+\dots + i_re_r, k+pf_m)
=
w(i_1e_1+\dots+ i_re_r, k)
\end{eqnarray*}
due to $p$-periodicity of $w$.
We also have
\begin{eqnarray*}
\mu_{(0,0),(i_1e_1+\dots + i_re_r, k+pf_m)}
&=&
\mu_{(0,0),(i_1e_1+\dots+ i_re_r, k)}\,
\tilde \psi_m (i_1e_1+\dots +i_re_r, k)
\\
&=&
\mu_{(0,0),(i_1e_1+\dots +i_re_r, k)}\,
\tilde \psi_m (0,0),
\end{eqnarray*}
since $\tilde \psi_m$ is constant on ${\mathbb Z}^{r+n}$.
The theorem is proved.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
\label{cor eigen}

Assume that the $p$-invariant discrete flat connection $(\varphi_l,\psi_m)$ is special.
Then the vector
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{ix0}
\phantom{aaa}
I(0)
&=&
\int w(j,0)\, dj
\\
\notag
&=&
\sum_{i_1, \dots, i_r=0}^{p-1}
w(i_1e_1+\dots + i_re_r,0)\ \mu_{(0,0),(i_1e_1+\dots + i_re_r,0)}
\end{eqnarray}
is an eigenvector of the $p$-curvature operators
$\left(C_m(0)\right)$ with respective eigenvalues $\left(\tilde \psi_m(0,0)\right)$.
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- rem-1: body_md -->
Given a $p$-invariant discrete flat connection $(L_m)$, one can construct flat eigensections of this connection whenever an integral representation of the type described in Section \ref{sec 3} is available.
Integral representations are known to exist for systems of rational qKZ difference
equations and for systems of qKZ difference equations associated with equivariant cohomology of Nakajima varieties.
If such a system is considered over a field of finite characteristic,
then the construction of Section \ref{sec 3} applies, and the corresponding flat eigensections can be obtained.



To keep the notation minimal, in this paper we focus on applications of the general construction
 to the rational qKZ discrete connection associated with a tensor product of Verma modules over $\mathfrak{gl}_2$ in characteristic $p$.
<!-- end rem-1 -->
<!-- exmp-1: body_md -->
The restriction of the rational $R$-matrix to the weight subspace
$\bigl(M_{\Lambda_1}\!\otimes M_{\Lambda_2}\bigr)\<\>[\<\>\Lambda_1\<+\Lambda_2\<-1,1\<\>]$
\,with the basis \,$fv_{\Lambda_1}\!\otimes v_{\Lambda_2}\,,\;v_{\Lambda_1}\!\otimes fv_{\Lambda_2}$
equals
\begin{equation*}
R_{\Lambda_1,\Lambda_2}(x)\,=\,\frac1{x-\Lambda_1}\,
\begin{pmatrix} x-\Lambda_1\<+\Lambda_2 & -\<\>\Lambda_2\\[4pt]
-\Lambda_1 & x \end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end exmp-1 -->
<!-- thm-3: body_md -->
\label{thm int rep}
There exist \(V\)-valued rational functions \(G_{l,m}(s,x)\)
for $l=1,\dots,r$ and $m=1,\dots,n$ in variables $s, x, a, \Lambda, \kappa$, such that
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{IR qkz}
&&
\Psi_m(s,x)\, W(s,x + af_m) 
\\
\notag
&&
\phantom{aaaa}
\,=\, K_m(x)W(s,x) \,+\,
\sum_{l=1}^r \left(\Phi_l(s,x)\,G_{l,m}(s+ae_l, x) - G_{l,m}(s,x)\right)
\end{eqnarray}
for $m=1,\dots,n$. Furthermore, the coordinate functions of every $G_{l,m}(s,x)$ in the basis $(f^{\vec r})$
are ratios $\frac{P(s,x)}{Q(s,x)}$\,,
where  $P(s,x)$ is a polynomial in $s,x, a,\Lambda, \kappa$
with integer coefficients, 
 and $Q(s,x)$ is a product of factors each of which is  of the form:
 \begin{align*}
s_k-x_i+ca\,, &\quad  k=1,\dots, r, \ i=1,\dots,n, 
\\
s_k-x_i + \Lambda_i +ca\,,  &\quad  k=1,\dots, r, \ i=1,\dots,n,
\\
s_k-s_j+ca \,,  &\quad k,j = 1,\dots, r,\ k\ne j,
\\
s_k-s_j + 1+ca\,,  &\quad k,j = 1,\dots, r,\ k\ne j,
\\
 x_i-x_m-\Lambda_i+ba,  &\quad   i,m=1,\dots,n, \ i\ne m,
 \\
 \kappa,&
\end{align*}
where $c\in {\mathbb Z}$, \ $b= 0, \dots, r-1$.\footnote{${}$ These factors (except $ x_i-x_m-\Lambda_i+ba$ and $\kappa$)
are 
the factors of the denominators of the functions 
$(\Phi_l, \Psi_m)$ in which variables $s$ and $x$ are shifted by integer multiples of $a$.}
<!-- end thm-3 -->
<!-- thm-4: body_md -->
\label{thm sing}
Set $\kappa=1$.
Then there exist  
\\
$\left(\bigotimes^n_{j=1} M_{{\Lambda_j}}\right)\left[\<\>\sum_{j=1}^n\Lambda_j-r+1,r-1\<\>\right]$-valued 
functions $H_l(s,x)$ for $l=1,\dots,r$,   rational  in variables $s,x,a,\Lambda$, such that
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{Si}
e\, W(s,x) \,= \,
\sum_{l=1}^r \left(\Phi_l(s,x)\,H_{l}(s+ae_l, x) - H_{l}(s,x)\right).
\end{eqnarray}
 Furthermore, the coordinate functions of every $H_{l}(s,x)$
   in the basis 
   $\{f^{\vec u}\}_{\vec u\in\mathcal I_{r-1}}$,
$u_1+\cdots+u_n=r-1,$
    of 
   $\left(\bigotimes^n_{j=1} M_{{\Lambda_j}}\right)\left[\<\>\sum_{j=1}^n\Lambda_j-r+1,r-1\<\>\right]$
are ratios 
$\frac{P(s,x)}{Q(s,x)}$\,,
where  $P(s,x)$ is a polynomial in $s,x, a,{\Lambda_1},\dots{\Lambda_n}$
with integer coefficients, 
 and $Q(s,x)$ is a product with factors each of which is  of the form 
$s_i-s_j$, where $i,j=1,\dots, r$, $i\ne j$.
<!-- end thm-4 -->
<!-- lem-4: body_md -->
\label{lem 4.2}
The $p$-curvature functions define automorphisms of the discrete flat connection $(K_{m,{\mathbb K}})$.
That is, for $1 \leqslant l, m \leqslant n$, we have:
\[
\tilde K_{l,{\mathbb K}}(x + af_m) K_{m,{\mathbb K}}(x) = K_{m,{\mathbb K}}(x) \tilde K_{l,{\mathbb K}}(x).
\]
Furthermore, the $p$-curvature functions mutually commute:
\[
\tilde K_{l,{\mathbb K}}(x) \tilde K_{m,{\mathbb K}}(x) = \tilde K_{m,{\mathbb K}}(x) \tilde K_{l,{\mathbb K}}(x).
\]
<!-- end lem-4 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
The lemma follows from the flatness conditions \eqref{ff qKZ}.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lem-5: body_md -->
\label{lem 5.1}
The $p$-curvature functions $\left(\tilde{\Phi}_{l,{\mathbb K}}(s,x),\tilde{\Psi}_{m,{\mathbb K}}(s,x)\right)$
are $a$-periodic in variables $s$ and $x$.
<!-- end lem-5 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
The lemma follows from the flatness conditions.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lem-6: body_md -->
\label{lem tilde}
The $p$-curvature functions $\left(\tilde{\Phi}_{l,{\mathbb K}}(s,x),\tilde{\Psi}_{m,{\mathbb K}}(s,x)\right)$ have the formulas:
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{phil K}
\tilde\Phi_{l,{\mathbb K}}(s\<\>,x) &=&
\kappa^p\,\prod_{i=1}^n\,\frac{h_p(s_l)-h_p(x_i)+h_p(\Lambda_i)}{h_p(s_l)-h_p(x_i)}\,\cdot\<\>
\prod_{j\ne l}\,\frac{h_p(s_l)-h_p(s_j)-h_p(1)}{h_p(s_l)-h_p(s_j)+h_p(1)}\;,
\\[4pt]
\label{psim K}
\tilde\Psi_{m,{\mathbb K}}(s\<\>,x) &=& \prod_{l=1}^r\,\frac{h_p(s_l)-h_p(x_m)}{h_p(s_l)-h_p(x_m)+h_p(\Lambda_m)}\;,
\end{eqnarray}
$l=1,\dots,r$, \;$m=1,\dots,n$\,, where $h_p(y) = y^p-a^{p-1}y$ is the
Artin–Schreier polynomial defined in Appendix \ref{app A}.
<!-- end lem-6 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
The lemma follows from formulas of Appendix \ref{app A}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- cor-2: body_md -->
\label{cor int}
Let $a, \kappa \in {\mathbb K}^\times$,\ $\Lambda_1$, \dots, $\Lambda_n\in {\mathbb K}$.
Then there exists $G_{l,m, {\mathbb K}}(s,x)$ for $l=1,\dots,r$, $m=1,\dots,n$, the
$V_{\mathbb K}$-valued rational functions in $(s,x)$, such that
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{I qkz}
&&
\Psi_{m, {\mathbb K}} (s,x)\, W_{\mathbb K}(s,x + af_m)
\\
\notag
&&
\,=\, K_{m,{\mathbb K}}(x)W_{\mathbb K}(s,x) \,+\,
\sum_{l=1}^r \left(\Phi_{l,{\mathbb K}}(s,x)\,G_{l,m,{\mathbb K}}(s+ae_l, x) - G_{l,m,{\mathbb K}}(s,x)\right)
\end{eqnarray}
for $m=1,\dots,n$.
Furthermore, each of the coordinate functions of every $G_{l,m,{\mathbb K}}(s,x)$ in the basis $(f^{\vec r})$
is a ratio $\frac{P(s,x)}{Q(s,x)}$\,,
where  $P(s,x)$ is a polynomial in $(s,x)$,
 and $Q(s,x)$ is a product with factors each of which is of the form:
  \begin{align*}
s_k-x_i+ca\,, &\quad  k=1,\dots, r, \ i=1,\dots,n, 
\\
s_k-x_i + \Lambda_i +ca\,,  &\quad  k=1,\dots, r, \ i=1,\dots,n,
\\
s_k-s_j+ca \,,  &\quad k,j = 1,\dots, r,\ k\ne j,
\\
s_k-s_j + 1+ca\,,  &\quad k,j = 1,\dots, r,\ k\ne j,
\\
 x_i-x_m-\Lambda_i+ba,  &\quad   i,m=1,\dots,n, \ i\ne m,
 \\
 \kappa,&
\end{align*}
where $c = 0, \dots, p-1$, \ $b= 0 \dots, r-1$.
<!-- end cor-2 -->
<!-- cor-3: body_md -->
\label{cor sing}
Set $\kappa=1$. Then there 
exist  $\left(\bigotimes^n_{j=1} M_{{\Lambda_j, {\mathbb K}}}\right)\!\left[\<\>\sum_{j=1}^n\Lambda_j-r+1,r-1\<\>\right]$-valued 
functions $H_{l,{\mathbb K}}(s,x)$ for $l=1,\dots,r$,   rational  in variables $s$ and $x$ such that
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{SiK}
e\, W_{\mathbb K}(s,x) \,=\, 
\sum_{l=1}^r \left(\Phi_{l,{\mathbb K}}(s,x)\,H_{l,{\mathbb K}}(s+ae_l, x) - H_{l,{\mathbb K}}(s,x)\right).
\end{eqnarray}
 Furthermore, the coordinate functions of every $H_{l,{\mathbb K}}(s,x)$ in the basis 
   in the basis 
   $\{f^{\vec u}\}_{\vec u\in\mathcal I_{r-1}}$,
$u_1+\cdots+u_n=r-1,$
    of 
   $\left(\bigotimes^n_{j=1} M_{{\Lambda_j}}\right)\left[\<\>\sum_{j=1}^n\Lambda_j-r+1,r-1\<\>\right]$
are ratios 
$\frac{P(s,x)}{Q(s,x)}$\,,
where  $P(s,x)$ is a polynomial in $(s,x)$, 
 and $Q(s,x)$ is the product of factors each of which has the form
 $s_i-s_j$, where $i,j=1,\dots, r$, $i\ne j$.
<!-- end cor-3 -->
<!-- lem-7: body_md -->
\label{IInt}

There exist $p$-periodic functions
\[
g_{l,m}:\mathbb Z^r\times\mathbb Z^n\to V_{\mathbb K},
\qquad l=1,\dots,r,\quad m=1,\dots,n,
\]
such that
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{II qkz}
\phantom{aaaaaa}
\psi_m(j,k)\, w(j,k + f_m) \,=\, L_m(k)w(j,k) \,+\,
\sum_{l=1}^r \left(\varphi_l(j,k)\,g_{l,m}(j+e_l, k) - g_{l,m}(j,k)\right)
\end{eqnarray}
for all $j\in{\mathbb Z}^r$, $k\in{\mathbb Z}^n$, $m=1,\dots,n$.
<!-- end lem-7 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
The functions $(g_{l,m})$ are just the liftings of the functions $(G_{l,m,{\mathbb K}})$ in Corollary \ref{cor int}.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- thm-5: body_md -->
\label{thm 5.6}

Let $(L_m)$ be associated with a solution $(s^0,x^0)$
to \eqref{bae 6}.
Define
a $V_{\mathbb K}$-valued function
$I : {\mathbb Z}^n \to V_{\mathbb K},$
by the formula:
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{ix3}
I(k)
&=&
\int w(j,k) dj\, .
\end{eqnarray}
Then the function $I$  is a flat section of the $p$-invariant discrete flat connection $(L_m)$,
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{ili 3}
I(k+f_m) = L_m(k) I(k),
\end{eqnarray}
for all $k\in{\mathbb Z}^n$ and $m=1,\dots, n$. Furthermore, the function $I$, if nonzero,  
is an eigensection of the $p$-curvature functions:
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{e so 3}
C_m(k)I(k) = \tilde \psi_m(0,0)I(k),
\end{eqnarray}
for $k\in{\mathbb Z}^n$ and $m=1,\dots,n$.

If $\kappa=1$, then the function $I:{\mathbb Z}^n \to V_{\mathbb K}$ takes values in ${\operatorname{Sing}} V_{\mathbb K}$, the singular vector subspace of $V_{\mathbb K}$.
<!-- end thm-5 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Formulas \eqref{ili 3} and \eqref{e so 3}
are the result of the application of Theorems \ref{thm sol} and \ref{thm i sol}
to $(L_m)$.
The last statement of the theorem means that 
\begin{eqnarray*}
e\,I(k) = 0, \qquad k\in{\mathbb Z}^n.
\end{eqnarray*}
That follows from Corollary \ref{cor sing} and Lemma \ref{lem int d}.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- cor-4: body_md -->
\label{cor m eigen}

Let $(s^0, x^0)$ be a solution to the system of Bethe ansatz equations:
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{BEA}
\kappa^p\,\prod_{i=1}^n\,\frac{h_p(s_l)-h_p(x_i)+h_p(\Lambda_i)}{h_p(s_l)-h_p(x_i)}\,\cdot\<\>
\prod_{j\ne l}\,\frac{h_p(s_l)-h_p(s_j)-h_p(1)}{h_p(s_l)-h_p(s_j)+h_p(1)}\,=\,1,
\end{eqnarray}
for $l=1,\dots, r$. Define a vector in $V_{\mathbb K}$,
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{mx0}
J(s^0,x^0)
&=&
\sum_{i_1, \dots, i_r=0}^{p-1}
W_{\mathbb K}(s^0 + a(i_1 e_1+\dots + i_r e_r), x^0)
\\
\notag
&&
\phantom{aa}
\times \ \
\prod_{l=1}^r\prod_{d_l=0}^{i_l-1}
\Phi_{l,{\mathbb K}}(s^0 + a(i_1e_1+\dots +i_{l-1}e_{l-1} +d_le_l), x^0).
\end{eqnarray}
Then $J(s^0,x^0)$, if nonzero, is an eigenvector of the $p$-curvature operators $\tilde K_{m,{\mathbb K}}(x^0)$,
$m=1,\dots,n$, with respective eigenvalues
\begin{equation}
\label{Mon psi}
\prod_{l=1}^r\,\frac{h_p(s_l^0)-h_p(x_m^0)}{h_p(s_l^0)-h_p(x_m^0)+h_p(\Lambda_m)}\,.
\end{equation}

Parallel transport of the fiber $V_{\mathbb K}$ over $x^0$ to the fibers over the points of the orbit $\mathcal O_{x^0}$
extends the vector $J(s^0,x^0)$ to a multi-valued section over $\mathcal O_{x^0}$ which is an eigensection of the
$p$-curvature functions $(\tilde K_{m,{\mathbb K}})$.
<!-- end cor-4 -->
<!-- lem-8: body_md -->
Under assumptions \eqref{7.2}, the function
\begin{equation*}
F(s\<\>,x)\,=\,\prod_{m=1}^n\,\prod_{l=1}^r\,g(s_l-x_m,\Lambda_{m})\,\cdot\<\>
\prod_{j\ne l}\,\bigl((s_l-s_j)\>g(s_l-s_j+1,-\<\>2)\bigr)\,,
\end{equation*}
is a polynomial in $s$ and $x$. Furthermore,
the function $F(s\<\>,x)$ is a master function for the connection 
$(\Phi_{l,{\mathbb K}}, \Psi_{m,{\mathbb K}})$ defined in Section \ref{sec 5.5},
 that is,
\begin{equation*}
\Phi_{l,{\mathbb K}}(s,x)\,=\,\frac{F(s + a e_l,x)}{F(s,x)}\;,
\qquad
\Psi_{m,{\mathbb K}}(s,x)\,=\,\frac{F(s, x+ af_m)}{F(s,x)}\;,
\end{equation*}
for $l=1,\dots,r$ and $m=1,\dots, n$.
<!-- end lem-8 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
The proof is by inspection.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- thm-6: body_md -->
\label{thm Lau}
For any $l_1,\dots,l_r\in {\mathbb Z}_{\geqslant 0}$, the $V_{\mathbb K}$-valued polynomial 
$Q_{pl_1+p-1,\dots,\>pl_r+p-1}(x)$ is a flat section
of the qKZ connection \eqref{Kmx},
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{flat lp}
Q_{pl_1+p-1,\dots,\>pl_r+p-1}( x+af_m) = K_m(x) Q_{pl_1+p-1,\dots,\>pl_r+p-1}(x), \quad m=1,\dots,n.
\end{eqnarray}
Furthermore, $Q_{kl_1,\dots,\>kl_r}(z)$ is an eigensection of the $p$-curvature operators with
all  eigenvalues equal to 1, that is,
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{7.4}
\tilde K_{m,{\mathbb K}}(x) \,Q_{pl_1+p-1,\dots,\>pl_r+p-1}(x) = Q_{pl_1+p-1,\dots,\>pl_r+p-1}(x),
\quad m=1,\dots,n.
\end{eqnarray}
Also,
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{7.5}
e\, Q_{pl_1+p-1,\dots,\>pl_r+p-1}= 0.
\end{eqnarray}
<!-- end thm-6 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Define
\begin{equation*}
I(s,x)\,=\!\sum_{j_1, \dots, j_r=0}^{p-1}
W_{\mathbb K}(s+a(j_1e_1+\dots +j_r e_r),x)\,F(s+a(j_1e_1+\dots +j_r e_r),x)\,.
\end{equation*}

On the one hand, it follows from the identities in Appendix \ref{app A},
that
\begin{eqnarray*}
I(s,x)\,= \! \sum_{l_1,\dots,l_r\in{\mathbb Z}_{\geqslant 0}}
Q_{pl_1+p-1,\dots,\>pl_r+p-1}(x) \,\prod_{i=1}^r h_p(s_i)^{l_i}
\end{eqnarray*}


On the other hand, by  Theorem \ref{thm 5.6},
the $V_{\mathbb K}$-valued polynomial
$I(s,x)$ is a flat section of the qKZ connection,
\begin{eqnarray*}
I(s,x+af_m)\,=\, K_{m,{\mathbb K}}(x) \,I(s,x), \qquad m=1,\dots,n.
\end{eqnarray*}

These two observations imply property  \eqref{flat lp}. Property
\eqref{7.4} follows from  Theorem \ref{thm i sol}. 
Property \eqref{7.5} holds since $\kappa=1$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- rem-2: body_md -->
Theorem \ref{thm Lau} was proved in \cite{MV1} for $\Lambda_i=1$, $i=1,\dots,n$, using a different construction. 
The polynomial 
flat sections $(Q_{pl_1+p-1,\dots,\>pl_r+p-1})$ were called in \cite{MV1} $p$-hypergeometric. See also \cite{MV2}.
<!-- end rem-2 -->
<!-- exmp-2: body_md -->
Assume that \,$\Lambda_{i}=1$ for $i=1,\dots,n$\,, and \,$r=1$\,. Let $a=-2$ and $n=2g+1$ for some positive integer $g$. Then Theorem
\ref{thm Lau} provides $g$ $p$-hypergeometric flat sections. They are linearly independent by \cite{MV2}.
<!-- end exmp-2 -->
<!-- lem-9: body_md -->
\label{lem orbits}
If $(s^0, x^0)$ is any solution to system \eqref{sba}, then the set of all  solutions to system
\eqref{sba} consists of the $p^r$ points\,:
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{orb s}
(s^0+a(i_1e_1+\dots+i_re_r), \ x^0+a(j_1f_1+\dots+j_n f_n)), 
\end{eqnarray}
where $0\leqslant  i_1,\dots,i_r, j_1,\dots,j_n \leqslant p-1.$\ 
In other words, the set of all solutions to system \eqref{sba} is the orbit $\mathcal O_{(s^0, x^0)}$
of the ${\mathbb Z}^{r}\times {\mathbb Z}^n$-action on ${\mathbb A}^{r}\times {\mathbb A}^n$.
<!-- end lem-9 -->
<!-- rem-3: body_md -->
System  \eqref{tba} arises in the XXX quantum integrable chains 
as the system of Bethe ansatz equations when
one diagonalizes the commuting transfer matrices  $(H_m)$. To every solution $(t^0,z^0)$ of that system, one assigns
an eigenvector of the transfer matrices with eigenvalues given by  the formula
$\left(\prod_{l=1}^r\,\frac{t_l-z_m}{t_l-z_m+\lambda_m}\right)\,.$
<!-- end rem-3 -->
<!-- cor-5: body_md -->
\label{cor B}

Let $(s^0,x^0)$ be a solution of the Bethe ansatz equation \eqref{BBAE}. 
Then $J(s^0,x^0)$,
whenever nonzero, is a common eigenvector of the $p$-curvature operators
$(\tilde K_{m,{\mathbb K}}(x^0))$, $m=1,\dots,n$, with eigenvalues
$(-\tilde\Psi_{m,{\mathbb K}}(s^0,x^0))$ given by~\eqref{Bsim K}.
<!-- end cor-5 -->
<!-- lem-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:B1}
For $i=1,\dots,n$ and $d=1,\dots,p-1$,
along the formal branch $s=s_i(\varepsilon)$, we have
$$\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}
\Phi_{1,{\mathbb K}}(s_i(\varepsilon)+aj,x^0)
=\mathcal O(\varepsilon^{p-d}).$$
 In particular, this product is $\mathcal O(\varepsilon)$.
<!-- end lem-10 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
By \eqref{a2}, all denominators occurring in the factors $\Phi_{1,{\mathbb K}}(s_i(\varepsilon)+aj,x^0)$ are nonzero at $(0,y_i^0)$. 
The factor with $j=0$ is $\mathcal O(\varepsilon^{p-1})$, while each factor with $1\leqslant j\leqslant d-1$ is $\mathcal O(\varepsilon^{-1})$. 


Multiplying all factors  gives
\[
\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}\Phi_{1,{\mathbb K}}(s_i(\varepsilon)+aj, x^0)
=
\mathcal O(\varepsilon^{p-1})\cdot\mathcal O(\varepsilon^{-1})^{d-1}
=
\mathcal O(\varepsilon^{p-d}).
\]
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lem-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:B2}

Since $W(s,x^0)$ is polynomial in $s$, the function $W(s_i(\varepsilon)+ad,x^0)$ is regular along the branch $s=s_i(\varepsilon)$
for $i=1,\dots, n$ and $d=0,\dots,p-1$.  The coordinates of $W(y_i^0,x^0)$ have the properties:
\begin{align}
W_j(y_i^0, x^0)
&=0,
\qquad
j>i,
\label{B15}
\\
W_i(y_i^0, x^0)
&=
\prod_{l<i}\!\left( x_i^0-\Lambda_i -x_l^0+\Lambda_l         \right)
\prod_{l>i}\!\left( x_i^0-\Lambda_i -x_l^0\right)
\ne0.
\label{B16}
\end{align}
<!-- end lem-11 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
For $j>i$, the first product defining $W_j$ contains the factor with $l=i$:$$s-x_i^0+\Lambda_i.$$At $s=y_i^0=x_i^0-\Lambda_i$, this factor is zero.
For $j=i$, neither product contains this vanishing factor, and the nonzero value is exactly \eqref{B16}.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- cor-6: body_md -->
\label{cor:lim}

For each $i=1,\dots,n$, the pullback  $J(s_i(\varepsilon),x^0)$
is regular at $\varepsilon=0$, and
$$
J(s_i(\varepsilon),x^0)
=
W(y_i^0,x^0)+\mathcal O(\varepsilon).
$$
The vectors $W(y_i^0,x^0)$, $i=1,\dots,n$, form a basis of $V_{\mathbb K}$.
<!-- end cor-6 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Along the branch $s=s_i(\varepsilon)$, the $d=0$ term in \eqref{mx1} is
$W(s_i(\varepsilon),x^0),$ which evaluates to $W(y_i^0,x^0)$ at $\varepsilon=0$.
 For every $d\geqslant 1$, Lemma \ref{lem:B1} gives$$\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}
\Phi_{1,{\mathbb K}}(s_i(\varepsilon)+aj,x^0)=\mathcal O(\varepsilon).$$
Since $W(s_i(\varepsilon)+ad,x^0)$ is regular, each term with $d\geqslant1$ tends to zero. Therefore$$J(s_i(\varepsilon),x^0)
=
W(y_i^0,x^0)+\mathcal O(\varepsilon).$$

The vectors $W(y_i^0,x^0)$ form a basis because the matrix of their coordinates in the basis$$f^{(1)},\dots,f^{(n)}$$is triangular with nonzero diagonal entries, by \eqref{B15} and \eqref{B16}.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- thm-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:basis}
Assume that ${\mathbb K}$ is algebraically closed. 
Assume \eqref{a1} and \eqref{a2}. 
Then for  generic $\kappa\in{\mathbb K}^\times$, equation \eqref{BBAE} has $n$ distinct solutions $s_1^0,\dots, s_n^0$, obtained by deforming the roots $y_1^0,\dots,y_n^0$, such that the corresponding vectors
$J(s^0_i,x^0)$, $i=1,\dots,n$, are nonzero and form a basis of $V_{\mathbb K}$.
Moreover, each $J(s_i^0,x^0)$ is a common eigenvector of the $p$-curvature 
operators $(\tilde K_{m,{\mathbb K}}(x^0))$ with respective eigenvalues
\[
-\,\frac{h_p(s_i^0-x_m^0)}{h_p(s_i^0-x_m^0+\Lambda_m)}\,,
\qquad m=1,\dots,n,
\]
that is, 
\begin{eqnarray*}
\tilde K_{m,{\mathbb K}}(x^0)J(s_i^0,x^0)
\,=\,
-\,\frac{h_p(s_i^0-x_m^0)}
        {h_p(s_i^0-x_m^0+\Lambda_m)}
J(s_i^0,x^0).
\end{eqnarray*}
<!-- end thm-7 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
For each $i=1,\dots,n$, let $s_i(\varepsilon)$ denote the formal branch of the
curve $X$ through $(0,y_i^0)$ constructed above. Thus
\[
F\bigl(\varepsilon,s_i(\varepsilon)\bigr)=0,
\qquad
s_i(0)=y_i^0,
\qquad
s_i(\varepsilon)=y_i^0+\mathcal O(\varepsilon^p).
\]
Since the points $y_1^0,\dots,y_n^0$ are pairwise distinct, these branches
are pairwise distinct.

Consider the fiber product
\[
Y=X\times_{\mathbb A^1_{\varepsilon}}\cdots
\times_{\mathbb A^1_{\varepsilon}}X,
\]
with coordinates $(\varepsilon,s_1,\dots,s_n)$, where each coordinate satisfies
$F(\varepsilon,s_i)=0$. Let
\[
Q_0=(0,y_1^0,\dots,y_n^0)\in Y.
\]
By the simplicity of the roots $y_i^0$, the projection
\[
\pi:Y\longrightarrow \mathbb A^1_{\varepsilon},
\qquad
(\varepsilon,s_1,\dots,s_n)\longmapsto\varepsilon,
\]
is etale in a neighborhood of $Q_0$. In particular, after replacing $Y$
by a sufficiently small open neighborhood of $Q_0$, the coordinates $s_i$
represent the $n$ branches chosen above.

By Corollary~\ref{cor:lim}, for each $i$ the pullback of
$J(s_i,x^0)$ to this neighborhood has a regular extension to $\varepsilon=0$,
and its value at $Q_0$ is
\[
J(s_i,x^0)\big|_{Q_0}=W(y_i^0,x^0).
\]
Define the determinant
\[
D
=
\det\bigl(J(s_1,x^0),\dots,J(s_n,x^0)\bigr),
\]
where the determinant is taken with respect to the basis
$f^{(1)},\dots,f^{(n)}$ of $V_{\mathbb K}$. Then $D$ is regular in a neighborhood of
$Q_0$, and
\[
D(Q_0)
=
\det\bigl(W(y_1^0,x^0),\dots,W(y_n^0,x^0)\bigr)\neq0,
\]
because the vectors $W(y_i^0,x^0)$ form a basis of $V_{\mathbb K}$ by
Corollary~\ref{cor:lim}.

Consequently, the nonvanishing locus
\[
Y_D=\{Q\in Y:D(Q)\neq0\}
\]
is a nonempty Zariski-open neighborhood of $Q_0$. Since $\pi$ is etale,
it is an open map on this neighborhood. Hence $\pi(Y_D)$ contains a
nonempty Zariski-open subset of the $\varepsilon$-line. For every $\varepsilon$ in this
open subset with $\varepsilon\neq0$, there is a point
\[
Q=(\varepsilon,s_1,\dots,s_n)\in Y_D.
\]
The numbers $s_1,\dots,s_n$ are distinct solutions of the Bethe ansatz
equation \eqref{BBAE}, obtained by deforming the roots
$y_1^0,\dots,y_n^0$, and
\[
D(Q)\neq0.
\]
Therefore the vectors
\[
J(s_1,x^0),\dots,J(s_n,x^0)
\]
are nonzero and form a basis of $V_{\mathbb K}$.

Since $\varepsilon=\kappa^{-1}$, a nonempty Zariski-open subset of the
$\varepsilon$-line away from $\varepsilon=0$ corresponds to a nonempty Zariski-open
subset of ${\mathbb K}^\times$ in the parameter $\kappa$. Thus the asserted basis
property holds for generic $\kappa\in{\mathbb K}^\times$.

Finally, by Corollary~\ref{cor B}, each vector $J(s_i,x^0)$ is a common
eigenvector of the $p$-curvature operators
$\tilde K_{m,{\mathbb K}}(x^0)$, with eigenvalue
\[
-\frac{h_p(s_i-x_m^0)}
       {h_p(s_i-x_m^0+\Lambda_m)}
\]
for $m=1,\dots,n$. This proves the theorem.
